new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the word (stem plus any enclitic, since -mo/-po and person markers shift stress rightward); secondary stress on alternate syllables leftward (fourth-from-last), except that in two-syllable reduplications the first syllable of the reduplicant takes secondary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Usually on the fourth-from-the-last syllable; in two-syllable reduplication the first syllable of the reduplicated portion attracts secondary stress even when it is fifth-from-last.
new_statements.exceptions: Two-syllable reduplication: the first syllable of the reduplicated portion attracts secondary stress whether it is fourth- or fifth-from-last (kampio-mpio [kaˌmpioˈmpio] 'firefly', kampa-kampaŋa [ˌkampakaˈmpaŋa] 'small branch'). Primary stress has no stated exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, including enclitics: the aspectual clitics -mo/-po (p. 34) and, per Mead & Truong 2021:61, person markers such as -no/-e 'precipitate stress movement', i.e. stress is assigned on the full stem+clitic string. Based on elicited word lists (814 items) from Kumbewaha village, August 2015; stress marked only where unpredictable.
new_statements.identity_note: Mead 2017 describes only the speech of Kumbewaha village (kecamatan Siotapina, kabupaten Buton), the eponymous and best-known variety of Kumbewaha [xks] / kumb1274. Mead & Truong 2021 find Kumbewaha 'more dialectally complex than previously recognized', with Wolowa (and probably Wakole) as further dialects, but state the same penultimate-stress rule holds across their whole Butonic data set including those lects. Hanan (2012-2014) treats Kumbewaha as a dialect of Cia-Cia [cia, ciac1237]; Mead and Ethnologue/Glottolog keep it a separate language.

sources.note: Appendix 4, pp. 60-61 (transcription conventions, illustrated with Lasalimu but stated to 'apply throughout the data set', which includes Kumbewaha, Wakole and Wolowa lects): primary stress on the penultimate syllable; two like vowels realised as one long vowel when the first is stressed; person/aspect markers (-no, -e, etc.) cause stress movement; secondary stress usually on fourth-from-last syllable, reduplication exception; unpredictable cases marked. Section 2.3 lists all prior Kumbewaha sources.

sources.note: Sister language Cia-Cia only: primary stress predictably penultimate, unaffected by weight or affixation, each vowel a stress-bearing unit (section 5.3, pp. 60-62). Mentions Kumbewaha only as an East Buton language (p. 13); no Kumbewaha data.
